spots.locationNote: On CA-78 ~2 mi S of Palo Verde store — effectively ON route (tomorrow's direction of travel), mi ~2600.7
spots.legalityNote: Established county park campground, ~18-20 first-come sites — legal
spots.cyclistIntel: Flush toilets, tables, fire rings, shade ramadas, 14-day limit. NO drinking water — buy at the Palo Verde store/bar 2 mi back before rolling in.
spots.seasonalNote: Snowbird arrivals begin in Nov but midweek space is near-certain

spots.name: Imperial Sand Dunes Rec Area (Glamis) — BLM
spots.priceNote: Permit fees ROSE Oct 1, 2025: $55/week off-site, $70/week on-site, $185/season, charged per street-legal 'primary vehicle' Oct 1-Apr 15. A bicycle is an edge case rangers may wave through, but don't bank on it
spots.locationNote: Route passes Glamis at ~mi 2640, 26 mi before Brawley
spots.legalityNote: Legal BLM camping with permit, but it's an OHV mega-area — camps are RV/toy-hauler flats
spots.cyclistIntel: NOT recommended: weekly-permit pricing is terrible value for one tent night, zero water, and Nov weekends bring wall-to-wall OHV noise. Push on to Brawley.
spots.seasonalNote: Nov 6, 2026 is a Friday — the dunes will be filling up with OHV crowds that evening

spots.name: Wiest Lake County Park
spots.priceNote: ~$30/night per recent camper reports; Imperial County publishes no online rate card — call (442) 265-1736 to confirm current tent rate
spots.locationNote: 5351 Dietrich Rd — ~6 mi N of Brawley via CA-111 N + Rutherford Rd; a real detour off the day's end point
spots.legalityNote: Imperial County officially lists both RV and TENT camping here — legal and current (county Public Works page)
spots.cyclistIntel: Lakeside grass, charcoal grills (no ground fires), clean bathrooms with showers per reviews — the only real tent camping in the Brawley area
spots.seasonalNote: Imperial Valley camping season is winter — open and pleasant in Nov

spots.name: Desert Trails RV Park & Golf Course
spots.priceNote: ~$37/night W/E sites reported (one caller quoted $45); ~100 tent sites per directory listings — call 760-352-7275 for the actual tent rate, which may come in under $35
spots.locationNote: 225 Wake Ave, south El Centro — on/near route at ~mi 2684, i.e. ~10 mi BEFORE the Calexico end point
spots.legalityNote: Private RV park that accepts tents (one of very few in Imperial Valley) — legal
spots.cyclistIntel: Showers, laundry, pool; last realistic camp before the border. Camp here and roll the final flat 10 mi into Calexico in the morning.
spots.seasonalNote: Winter-season park — fully open in Nov, snowbirds arriving

spots.name: Elliot Mine Area Dispersed Camping (BLM)
spots.priceNote: Free BLM dispersed camping, 14-day limit
spots.locationNote: Approx coords — dispersed area ~1.1 mi off route near Jacumba; verify exact BLM parcel boundary before pitching
spots.legalityNote: Dispersed camping on BLM land is legal (14-day limit, pack out everything). Legality depends on being on the BLM parcel, not adjacent private/railroad land — could not verify parcel lines. Heavy Border Patrol activity in this corridor; expect vehicle passes at night.
spots.cyclistIntel: Zero facilities, zero water — tank up in Jacumba town first. Only worth it if DeAnza is full/closed; the hotel pools in town are a better evening anyway.
spots.seasonalNote: High desert ~2,800 ft — Nov nights near freezing

spots.name: DeAnza Springs Resort
spots.priceNote: Dry tent sites — nightly rate not published (weekly is $155, so figure ~$25–35/night); book via Campspot or call
spots.locationNote: 1951 Carrizo Gorge Rd, ~2–3 mi north of Jacumba town via Carrizo Gorge Rd (approx coords)
spots.legalityNote: Legal private campground/resort, 311+ RV sites plus dedicated dry tent sites
spots.cyclistIntel: Best facilities anywhere near Jacumba: two pools (one heated/enclosed year-round), hot tub, showers, cafe, wifi. HEADS-UP: this was famously a clothing-optional/nudist resort for decades; current ownership's website no longer mentions that policy — call ahead to confirm the vibe before committing.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round; high desert 2,600 ft, cold nights in Nov

spots.name: Boulevard / Cleveland National Forest KOA Journey
spots.priceNote: Tent sites est. $35–45/night — KOA site blocked automated verification; call for current rate
spots.locationNote: 2299 Ribbonwood Rd, Boulevard — just off Old Hwy 80 route through Boulevard (approx coords)
spots.legalityNote: Legal private KOA campground with tent sites
spots.cyclistIntel: 40-acre KOA with showers, store, stargazing area; 9 mi past Jacumba essentially ON route, so it shortens Day 50. Solid plan-B if DeAnza doesn't suit.
spots.seasonalNote: Believed open year-round — confirm by phone; ~3,400 ft, freezing Nov nights possible

spots.name: Lark Canyon Campground (BLM McCain Valley)
spots.priceNote: $6/site/night, first-come, 15 sites
spots.locationNote: 4.2 mi off route up McCain Valley Rd from Boulevard (net climb); OHV area adjoins campground
spots.legalityNote: Established BLM fee campground — fully legal, 14-day limit
spots.cyclistIntel: Cheapest legal roof-of-nothing in the area, but it's 13 mi PAST the Jacumba day-end plus a 4.2-mi side climb. Water on site is NOT tested safe for drinking — carry from Boulevard. Vault toilets, fire rings, tables. Can be noisy with OHVs on weekends; Nov 8 is a Sunday night so it should empty out.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round; ~4,000 ft elevation, cold Nov nights

spots.name: Green Valley Campground (Cuyamaca Rancho State Park)
spots.priceNote: $40/night/site standard (per site, not per person); no hike/bike site at this park
spots.locationNote: 3.2 mi off route up Hwy 79 from the Descanso area; 15 mi BEFORE the Alpine day-end
spots.legalityNote: State park campground — fully legal
spots.cyclistIntel: Pretty oak/creek setting, flush toilets, pay showers. Booking is via ReserveCalifornia but a Monday night in November will have walk-up room. Costs you 15 route miles + a 3.2-mi climb off route, making Day 51 to Encinitas very long.
spots.seasonalNote: Vehicle-access camping season runs Apr 1 – Nov 30, so OPEN Nov 9 — one of its last weeks of the season. ~4,000 ft: expect nights near/below freezing.

spots.name: Lake Jennings Campground
spots.priceNote: Standard tent (non-hookup) $45 Sun–Thu / $50 Fri–Sat (rates effective May 2025); Nov 9 is a Monday = $45
spots.locationNote: 9535 Harritt Rd, Lakeside — ~5–6 mi past Alpine along the route toward El Cajon, ~1 mi off
spots.legalityNote: Legal established campground (Helix Water District park)
spots.cyclistIntel: Hot showers, store, lake views, walk-in tent-only sites available; 44 non-hookup tent sites so midweek Nov availability is easy. Sleeping here instead of before Alpine shaves 5+ mi off the long Day 51 into Encinitas.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round; mild low-elevation nights

spots.name: San Elijo State Beach — Hike & Bike site
spots.priceNote: Hike/bike $15/person/night (raised from $10 — verified on parks.ca.gov Aug 2026); shared site #94, pay on arrival
spots.locationNote: 2050 S Coast Hwy 101, Cardiff-by-the-Sea — directly ON route, 2.7 mi before the Encinitas day-end
spots.legalityNote: Official CA State Parks hike & bike program — arrive by bike, no reservation possible or needed
spots.cyclistIntel: THE classic Pacific Coast route stop: blufftop over the surf, hot pay showers (bring quarters), flush toilets, market/taco shops across Hwy 101. Registration after 2 PM, vacate by noon; max 2 consecutive nights, 10 hike/bike days per calendar year statewide. November midweek = the shared site will very likely be yours alone.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round; hike/bike is first-come and effectively never full in Nov

spots.name: San Elijo State Beach — standard tent site (fallback)
spots.priceNote: Standard sites roughly $40–60/night per site depending on location; reserve on ReserveCalifornia
spots.locationNote: Same campground as the hike/bike site
spots.legalityNote: State beach campground — fully legal
spots.cyclistIntel: Only needed if the hike/bike site somehow can't take you (it will in November).
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round

spots.name: South Carlsbad State Beach — Hike & Bike site
spots.priceNote: Historically has hike/bike sites; assume $15/person matching the statewide rate — UNVERIFIED for 2026
spots.locationNote: 7201 Carlsbad Blvd — ON route, 3.2 mi past the Encinitas day-end
spots.legalityNote: State beach campground; hike/bike arrival by bicycle only
spots.cyclistIntel: Blufftop campground similar to San Elijo. RED FLAG: reservation systems showed NO upcoming availability at South Carlsbad as of Aug 2026 — this campground has long-rumored bluff/utility closure plans. Call the kiosk (760-438-3143) before counting on it; treat San Elijo as the sure thing.
spots.seasonalNote: Possible full-campground closure in late 2026 — verify by phone

spots.name: San Onofre State Beach — San Mateo Campground (early alternative)
spots.priceNote: Standard non-hookup est. ~$40/site (tent-only loop sites 101–157 may run less — verify on ReserveCalifornia)
spots.locationNote: 830 Cristianitos Rd, San Clemente — ~1.5 mi inland off route, ~34 mi before Newport Beach
spots.legalityNote: State beach campground, open YEAR-ROUND (verified). NOTE: the other San Onofre campground — Bluffs — is CLOSED to camping Oct 1–May 15, so it is NOT an option on Nov 11.
spots.cyclistIntel: Hot showers, drinking water, flush toilets. Really only useful as a bail-out if you're cooked coming off the Camp Pendleton bike path — it leaves 87 mi to Santa Monica.
spots.seasonalNote: San Mateo open year-round; Bluffs closed in November. SEPARATE ISSUE: Camp Pendleton recreational bicycle passes are SUSPENDED as of Aug 2026 - plan the outside-the-fence routing (coastal path San Onofre to Las Pulgas, then the bicycle-legal I-5 shoulder into Oceanside). Re-check with the Visitor Center, 760-763-8435.

spots.name: San Clemente State Beach
spots.priceNote: Tent campsite $45–50/night (parks.ca.gov); a hike/bike site has historically existed here (~$15/pp) but is unverified — call the park pass office
spots.locationNote: Blufftop off Avenida Calafia, San Clemente — ~1 mi off route, ~29 mi before Newport Beach
spots.legalityNote: State beach campground — fully legal
spots.cyclistIntel: Fine campground but Doheny 7 mi further is flatter, cheaper for a cyclist, and confirmed bike-friendly — skip unless timing forces it.
spots.seasonalNote: Generally open year-round — confirm

spots.name: Doheny State Beach — Hike & Bike site
spots.priceNote: Hike/bike area confirmed by the touring community as welcoming; price assumed $15/person matching statewide rate (official pages list only standard $50 / beachfront $65 sites) — call to confirm
spots.locationNote: 25300 Dana Point Harbor Dr, Dana Point — ON route, ~22 mi before the Newport Beach day-end
spots.legalityNote: State beach campground with hike/bike arrival by bicycle
spots.cyclistIntel: Classic Pacific Coast overnight: flat beachside camp, hot showers, staff historically friendly to touring cyclists. Trade-off: stopping here makes Day 52 short (~40 mi) and the final Santa Monica day long (~74 mi).
spots.seasonalNote: Campground open year-round; Nov midweek wide open

spots.name: Crystal Cove State Park — Lower Moro primitive camp
spots.priceNote: Primitive hike-in site, est. ~$25/night/site (unverified — check ReserveCalifornia); listed with hike/bike among its site types
spots.locationNote: ~2 mi UP Moro Ridge Trail (dirt) from the PCH trailhead — approx coords; 10 mi before Newport Beach
spots.legalityNote: Legal state park primitive campground; reservation via ReserveCalifornia
spots.cyclistIntel: Closest cheap-ish camp to Newport, BUT: 2-mi climb on dirt with a loaded touring bike, NO water (haul it up), vault toilet only, no fires. Ocean-view sunrise is the payoff. Only choose this over Doheny if you want the endpoint miles.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round, weather permitting

spots.name: Crystal Cove State Park — Moro Campground (developed)
spots.priceNote: Non-hookup 'low impact' tent sites — reported range $25–75/night by season; expect ~$45 off-season, reserve online
spots.locationNote: Blufftop above PCH at El Moro — ON route, 10 mi before Newport Beach
spots.legalityNote: State park campground — fully legal; NO dedicated hike/bike site at the developed campground (only the Lower Moro primitive area carries a hike/bike designation)
spots.cyclistIntel: Full-service blufftop camp with showers and ocean views, no hike-a-bike required — the comfort play if you'd rather pay ~$45 than climb to Lower Moro.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round

spots.name: Dockweiler RV Park (LA County)
spots.priceNote: RV sites roughly $45–75/night — IRRELEVANT FOR TENTS: verified NO tent camping, RVs/camper vans only
spots.locationNote: 12001 Vista del Mar, Playa del Rey — on the beach bike path ~9 mi before the pier
spots.legalityNote: VERIFIED: LA County rules prohibit tent camping and overnight outdoor sleeping — self-contained RVs/camper vans only. The only beach 'camping' in LA County, but a tent tourer cannot legally stay here.
spots.cyclistIntel: Do not route your last night around this one — county rules explicitly bar sleeping outside an RV. It only works if you somehow have vehicle support meeting you.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round

spots.name: HI Los Angeles — Santa Monica Hostel
spots.priceNote: Dorm beds typically ~$37–60/night in November (rates float; book online early)
spots.locationNote: 1436 2nd St, Santa Monica — 2 blocks from the pier finish line
spots.legalityNote: Hostel — indoor dorm bed, no tent needed
spots.cyclistIntel: The only true budget bed at the finish; big touring-cyclist tradition to end here. Book a few days out — even Nov weeknights can fill. Ask about bike storage when booking (not confirmed on their site).
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round

spots.name: Big Lagoon State Park
spots.priceNote: FL state-park campsites run $16-42/night + tax and reservation fee; primitive camping statewide is $5/person where offered. Call for the current site rate.
spots.locationNote: 12301 Gulf Beach Hwy, ~10 mi west of downtown Pensacola - the first campground on the route, ~31 mi before the Day 1 endpoint.
spots.legalityNote: Florida State Parks operate a formal NO-TURN-AWAY policy for self-contained cyclists: a full campground must still take you. Adventure Cycling maintains the policy list - carry a copy or screenshot.
spots.cyclistIntel: Only useful if Day 1 gets cut short by a late start, weather, or a shakedown problem with the rig. Florida is also the one state on the route with a statewide public-camping ban (2024 HB 1365), so this park is the legal option near Pensacola rather than one of several.
spots.seasonalNote: Open year-round; post-Labor Day availability is good.

spots.name: Franklinton Police Dept — 17 mi OFF ROUTE (bail-out only)
spots.priceNote: Free with permission.
spots.locationNote: NOT ON YOUR LINE. Your route runs through Bogalusa (mi 250); Franklinton sits ~17 mi north, so this is a ~34-mi round trip. The mile number below is where it projects onto the route, NOT how far you ride to reach it. Listed because it is a confirmed free indoor-shower host on the classic ACA alignment.
spots.legalityNote: Explicit permission from the on-duty officer; the department is listed as a cyclist host on ACA addenda.
spots.cyclistIntel: Tent on the grass behind the station with access to an indoor bathroom WITH SHOWER and the kitchen. A March 2025 westbound group called it excellent. Only worth the 34-mi round trip if Day 4 falls apart - otherwise note that Bogalusa is the on-route town.

spots.name: Bunkie Fire Station
spots.priceNote: Free. House rule: cyclists must shower.
spots.locationNote: Bunkie town center, dead on route - ~25 mi into Day 10, 39 mi before the Mamou endpoint.
spots.legalityNote: Firefighters host cyclists by long-standing local custom - walk in and ask the on-duty crew.
spots.cyclistIntel: You sleep INDOORS on the station couches with bathroom and kitchen access - not a tent site. A rider stayed in March 2025 and the tradition goes back years in ST notes. This is the strongest wet-weather option between Simmesport and Mamou, worth remembering when a Gulf storm is chasing you.

spots.name: Allen Parish Tourist Commission - field behind the office
spots.priceNote: Free.
spots.locationNote: 8904 Hwy 165, Oberlin - dead on route, ~25 mi into Day 11 and 37 mi before the DeRidder endpoint.
spots.legalityNote: Parish-sanctioned cyclist camping; the tourist commission lists it and it appears on Warmshowers. Arrive during office hours to check in.
spots.cyclistIntel: Tent in the field behind the tourism office with SHOWERS ON SITE - rare for a free stop. A March 2025 westbound group camped here and the local VFW president brought them gumbo dinner. Allen Parish actively courts Southern Tier riders. Food: Landreneaus Cafe & Grocery and a Dollar General in town. Skip the local motel per ACA's own note.

spots.name: Atakapa-Coushatta Trace Visitors Center (Merryville)
spots.priceNote: Free; officially listed by the parish under 'Cyclist Camping'.
spots.locationNote: 703 N. Bryan St, Merryville - second free option in town alongside the museum, ~19 mi into Day 12.
spots.legalityNote: Beauregard Parish Tourist Commission lists it as cyclist camping: TENTS ONLY, 2-night maximum, shower house on site.
spots.cyclistIntel: The backup if the Historical Society Museum's cyclist cabin is taken or nobody answers. Two independent free options in one village of 1,100 makes Merryville the most reliable free stop on the eastern half.

spots.name: Shepherd Sanctuary
spots.priceNote: $10 per 24-hour tent site (official rates page); cabins also offered, with a cyclist discount reported.
spots.locationNote: 1445 Shraderville Rd, Shepherd - dead on route, ~56 mi into Day 14 and 14 mi before the Coldspring endpoint.
spots.legalityNote: Private rustic campground and retreat; books cyclists directly.
spots.cyclistIntel: Repeatedly hosts Southern Tier groups - two separate 2025 westbound journals stayed, one taking cabins and using the warm common room to dry out. Cell service is poor, so call before you're out of signal. At $10 it is the cheapest roofed-or-tented option in this stretch of East Texas.

spots.name: Pecos River picnic area (US 90, west of the high bridge)
spots.priceNote: Free - TxDOT picnic area, no fee, no host.
spots.locationNote: US 90 just west of the Pecos River high bridge, on a 0.6-mi loop off the highway - ~54 mi into Day 24, 2 mi past Seminole Canyon SP.
spots.legalityNote: Texas Transp. Code 545.411 allows up to 24 hours at any TxDOT picnic area, roadside park, or overlook. Erecting a tent is prohibited on paper, but an offense requires a posted sign or an officer's notice plus 8 hours to comply - riders routinely cowboy-camp or pitch late and strike early.
spots.cyclistIntel: Covered stone tables on the canyon rim; RVs and semis overnight here routinely so a bike is unremarkable. NO WATER and no toilets - fill at Seminole Canyon SP two miles back, which is the last reliable water before Langtry. The free alternative to paying at Seminole Canyon if you only need a flat spot.
spots.seasonalNote: Exposed - wind and lightning are the real hazards here, not people.

spots.name: First Baptist Church of Sanderson
spots.priceNote: Free with permission; leave a donation.
spots.locationNote: In Sanderson, essentially on the Day 25/26 boundary - the town is your D25 endpoint area and D26 start.
spots.legalityNote: Pastor's permission. Call ahead - the church is reachable on Facebook, or go through the Terrell County Visitor Center (432-345-2324, Wed-Sat 12-5).
spots.cyclistIntel: A March 2025 westbound group slept INSIDE the church, showered at the pastor's house, and was fed a spaghetti dinner by the pastor's wife plus breakfast the next morning. Two independent 2025 journals record it. Note there is NO breakfast spot in Sanderson - carry food out regardless.
spots.seasonalNote: Wednesday evenings have church activities; avoid occupying a fellowship hall Saturday night without explicit blessing.

spots.name: Boulder Oaks Campground (Cleveland NF)
spots.priceNote: $5/night WALK-IN sites (standard drive-in sites $20). Reservable on recreation.gov; walk-ins first-come.
spots.locationNote: Old Hwy 80 at Buckman Springs Rd (I-8 exit 51) - directly ON route, ~29 mi into Day 50 and ~27 mi before the Alpine endpoint.
spots.legalityNote: Developed Forest Service campground, so no remote-camping permit needed. Note Cleveland NF bans wood and charcoal fires outside developed campgrounds and requires a free permit for dispersed camping elsewhere in the district.
spots.cyclistIntel: The best-value night on the California leg: $5 with POTABLE WATER, on the Pacific Crest Trail, and dead on your line - compared with $40 at Green Valley in Cuyamaca, which also costs 15 route miles and a 3.2-mi climb. Vault toilets, no showers.
spots.seasonalNote: Seasonal arroyo-toad closures affect this campground in spring and summer; a fall passage should be open but VERIFY before relying on it.

dayAdvice.gapAdvice: The planned endpoint (mi 78.1) sits in a camping dead zone between the Gulf Shores cluster (mi 60-69) and the ferry (mi ~86). Best play: lengthen ~9 mi, catch the LAST 3:30 PM ferry from Fort Morgan (departures 8:00/10:30/1:00/3:30; bikes free, pedestrian fare ~$5-10; verify at mobilebayferry.com, (251) 540-7787) and camp at Dauphin Island Campground for $22 — you also bank the crossing against morning weather cancellation. If you can't make 3:30, call Fort Morgan RV Park (pricey) for the 8:00 AM boat, or shorten to Gulf State Park's $25 primitive loop and ride 25 mi to the 10:30 AM ferry. || ALSO: Big Lagoon State Park sits at mi 47 (~31 mi before this endpoint) — too early to show in this day's list, but it is the legal bail-out if a late start, weather, or a shakedown problem with the can rig cuts Day 1 short. Florida's no-turn-away policy means a full campground still has to take you. (850) 492-1595.

Pascagoula itself has no legal campground — plan on Shepard SP 5 mi ahead in Gautier ($13 primitive) or push 17 mi to Davis Bayou. The OSM 'RV Campground' at mi 153.8 is Indian Point RV Resort (Gautier, $40/night) which is RVs-ONLY, no tents — skip it.

Diamondhead proper has no campground, and Hollywood Casino RV Park (Bay St. Louis) is RVs-only. McLeod ($35, 4-5 mi away, no backtrack) is the practical pick; Buccaneer's $20 primitive area saves $15 but costs a ~20-mi round-trip detour off the inland reroute. Decide by legs, not wallet.

Thin day. Bogalusa has NO legal camping (Cassidy Park is day-use only). Call Berry Creek from Bogalusa; if no answer or no tents, the honest choices are the 13-mi detour to Bogue Chitto SP or riding +20 to Fontainebleau's first-come tent sites ($18-27) — the latter also turns Day 5 into an easy ~52-mi cruise into New Orleans.

There is no camping in New Orleans proper — every tent option overshoots or detours: Bayou Segnette ($33+tax, cross via Algiers Point ferry then ~10 mi), St. Bernard SP ($28, 18 mi SE), KOA ($60+). For a rest day IN the city, India House Hostel (~$29-40 dorm, Mid-City, (504) 821-1904) beats the ferry-and-ride logistics and costs about the same as a Friday-night state-park site; HI New Orleans and The Quisby run ~$40+. If camping matters more than the city, book Bayou Segnette online before arrival — Friday nights fill.

Donaldsonville has NO verified tent camping. Realistic plays: (1) call B&B RV Park about pitching a tent; (2) ask at a Donaldsonville church or the police department about Crescent Park/Louisiana Square — classic Louisiana small-town move but unverified here; (3) restructure days 6-7 so the overnight lands at Port Allen (Cajun Country CG, mile ~437) or Farr Park ($10 dry camp) — both verified, ~35 route mi past Donaldsonville, which shortens Day 7 into St. Francisville to ~30 mi. Water/food resupply in Donaldsonville is good either way.

The two Tunica Hills options are a serious 14-15 mi hilly detour NW; if you want to stay on-line, either call Shelby J's about a tent spot near the bridge or push 11 mi to Jim's Camping Area on False River.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Maxey Care RV Park and Campground
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Call Maxey Care in advance about tents (225-694-3929); if no, Jim's at mile 480.6 is the verified-tent fallback.

Genuinely anchor-less: no verified commercial campground within the flex window. Plan to sleep in/near Simmesport (mile ~525) rather than the literal mile-527 endpoint. Pre-trip, call Avoyelles tourism (318-964-2025) to confirm Yellow Bayou camping; on the day, top off water in Simmesport (last services). Paid fallbacks are all off-route: Marksville (17 mi N, motels + Paragon Casino RV Resort — RV-oriented, tents doubtful). Avoid Atchafalaya-area WMA land unless you've bought the Wild Louisiana Stamp and confirmed a designated camping area — most nearby WMA ground is seasonal-hunt land with no designated sites on the route. || UPDATE 2026-08-27: this is no longer a true gap. A Simmesport church sheltered a westbound group for two storm nights in March 2025 and hosted a separate solo ST rider the same week - ask at First Baptist or the Methodist church, or at town hall. ALSO WORTH DOING: Day 8 is only 21 mi and Day 9 is 37, so St. Francisville to Simmesport is one reasonable 53-mi day. Merging them frees a whole calendar day against the zero-spare-days problem.

Cleanest plan: end Day 10 at Chicot SP (mile ~578) instead of Mamou and absorb the extra ~14 mi into Day 11. || MID-DAY SHELTER: the Bunkie FIRE STATION at mi 552 (~39 mi before this endpoint, so it does not appear in the list below) puts you INDOORS on the station couches with bathroom and kitchen — free, confirmed March 2025, one house rule: you must shower. This is the wet-weather escape hatch on Day 10 if a Gulf storm is chasing you. Walk in and ask the crew.

Strong recommendation: ride the extra 18 mi to the Merryville Museum — free/donation, tents welcome, showers, cabin option, and it sets up the Texas-line crossing next morning. If ending in DeRidder proper, call Big Oak ($20) about tents first; DeRidder's West Park has restrooms/pavilion but no sanctioned camping (city parks dept 337-462-8900 if stuck). Sam Houston Jones SP is 40+ mi south — not viable. || WORTH SHORTENING THE DAY FOR: the Allen Parish Tourist Commission in OBERLIN, mi 616 (~37 mi before this endpoint), lets cyclists tent in the field behind the office WITH SHOWERS ON SITE — free, confirmed March 2025, when the local VFW president brought the riders gumbo. Showers on a free night are rare enough to be worth ending Day 11 early. (337) 639-4868, arrive during office hours.

No verified campground exists in or near Kirbyville itself. Plan A: call the Kirbyville Methodist/Baptist churches a day ahead (long-standing rider tradition). Plan B: stop 20 mi early at the Merryville Museum cyclist camp (free, cabin possible) and ride a longer Day 13. Plan C: Kirbyville's small motel. Check Warmshowers for the Kirbyville-area host seen in journals.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Village Creek State Park (Creekside hike-in sites)
Double Lake Recreation Area (Sam Houston NF)
Buescher State Park (Oak Haven / Lakeview / primitive walk-in)

dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Pecan Grove RV Park (0.2 mi off, Barton Springs Rd) is RVs ONLY — no tents, sites to $80, so skip it. HI Austin (Lakeshore Blvd) no longer appears in current listings and is believed permanently closed — Firehouse Hostel is the working hostel fallback. Warning: ACL Fest (typically Oct weekends 1-2 at Zilker, i.e. right at your Oct 8 arrival) jacks up every downtown bed — camp at McKinney Falls to stay insulated.

Johnson City proper is now a tent DESERT: Roadrunner RV Park (mi 1119.2, the old ST standby) is RV/cabin only (30A from $45, cabins $65, no tents per its own site), Johnson City RV Park is a $70-80 'boutique' RV-only park, and Flat Creek Crossing Ranch (mi 1101.6) has SUSPENDED all tent/RV camping until further notice. LBJ National Historical Park and LBJ State Park (Stonewall) are day-use, no camping. Practical plan: reserve Pedernales Falls and peel off before town, or budget-bust at Miller Creek. Cash-strapped riders have historically asked at JC churches — unverified, ask locally, never assume.

The RV-park cluster on the OSM hints is mostly useless for tents: Buckhorn Lake Resort and Guadalupe River RV Resort are big-rig luxury resorts, and Take-It-Easy (mi 1182.4) is a 55+ RV community — none confirm tents. Kerrville-Schreiner is the obvious answer; book the Saturday night early.

Foxfire Cabins (1 mi S of the SNA on the Sabinal) is cabins-only — no tent sites — and runs multi-night minimums in leaf season; treat as a splurge/bad-weather bail only. If everything at Vanderpool is somehow full, Utopia (~16 mi south, off route) has lodging, and Leakey (17 mi ahead over the big 337 climbs) has commercial camps — but on a Sunday night the private Lost Maples RV almost certainly has a $15 primitive spot; call (830) 966-3912 a few days out.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Nueces River RV and Cabin Resort (formerly Big Oak River Camp)
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Camp Wood remains one of the friendliest cheap-camping towns on the Texas ST — three legal riverfront options within 4 miles. Resupply and top off water here: the next day westward is the famously brutal, service-free stretch toward Brackettville/Del Rio.

The mapped endpoint sits by Laughlin AFB, and the FamCamp there is restricted to military/DoD ID holders (active, guard, reserve, retired, DAV, DoD civilians) — EXCLUDED for a civilian rider, and there is no other camping at that exact point. Real choices: (a) push 8-12 extra miles through Del Rio to Hidden Valley (~$20, town services) or on to Amistad's Governors Landing ($6-10, water on site, FCFS, no showers); (b) stop 30 mi short at Fort Clark Springs; or (c) motel row in Del Rio. Whatever you pick, leave Del Rio with maximum water — Amistad campgrounds other than Governors Landing are dry, and so is the road to Comstock.

Arrive in Langtry before 5pm to load water at the visitor center. If the community center situation has changed, backtrack is impossible - so if in doubt, commit to Seminole Canyon (mile 1398.5) instead and ride a longer Day 25.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Terrell County Visitor Center / picnic area grounds
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Budget Inn Sanderson (US 90 west side, ~$55-70) is the cheap roof fallback. Sanderson has a grocery (Stripes/Family Dollar) - resupply here, the next 71 mi to Marathon are empty.
Gage Gardens is a private hotel garden - no camping. If La Loma is full/closed, Marathon Motel's $15 tent sites are the sure thing.

The OSM 'Dispersed Camping Marfa' node at mile 1597.9 could not be verified as legal camping - likely an informal roadside pullout; skip it. El Cosmico is closed. If everything in Marfa is full (event weekend), Alpine at mile 1581 is the pressure valve.

Valentine has NO motel, store, or restaurant - carry dinner/breakfast and full water from Marfa. Sunday arrival means arrange school permission by phone Friday, or knock at the church/post office - locals are used to Southern Tier riders. Prada Marfa (mile ~1645) is an art installation, not a campsite. Fallbacks: book a Love Shak, backtrack nothing (Marfa is 36 mi behind), or grind 38 more mi to Van Horn RV Park - not recommended after a 40-mi day.

No RV park in Sierra Blanca itself takes tents (nothing verified operating). If the public park feels wrong, Sierra Blanca has budget motels (Americana Inn, ~$50-60). Load ALL water in Van Horn - the 35 mi between have zero services, and the I-10 frontage climb is exposed.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Fort Hancock Community Church (18 mi before Fabens)
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Fabens itself has NO verified legal camping - this is the segment's real gap. Best plays: (1) shorten the day and camp at Fort Hancock Community Church (mile ~1772) with permission - the established cyclist move; (2) take a roof night: Fabens Inn, 1884 Fabens Rd near I-10, ~$79/night (reviews warn of surprise fees - confirm total price at check-in), or Fort Hancock Motel ~$60-70; (3) push ~20 more miles into El Paso's Mission Valley where motels are plentiful. Do not stealth camp in the irrigated farm strip - it is all private land near the border with heavy Border Patrol presence.

Honest gap: the Anthony/La Union/Canutillo area has no true tent campground on-route. La Viña Winery (4201 NM 28, right at the day's endpoint) is a tasting room only — no camping offered (it does host an early-Oct wine festival; don't count on pitching there). Best plays: (1) call El Paso West RV Park and confirm a tent spot; (2) push ~15 flat miles up NM 28 to Mesilla/Las Cruces — Las Cruces has an active Warmshowers community and budget motels on Picacho Ave/S Valley Dr around $55-75; (3) motels cluster at the I-10 Anthony exit (~$55-70). Some riders simply combine this into a long day to Leasburg Dam SP (44 mi ahead, $20 guaranteed legal camping).

City of Rocks SP is ~25+ mi off-corridor east — skip it. Silver City is a Continental Divide Trail gateway town and generally friendly to dusty travelers, but it has no official free hiker/biker camp in town — the visitor center or Gila Hike & Bike (local shop) are the right places to ask about current CDT-er crash options if you want to overnight in town instead.

If the free gravel lot doesn't appeal after six desert days, Lordsburg's aging I-10 motels (Econo Lodge etc.) run ~$50-70 and the KOA's tent sites ~$35 buy a hot shower and laundry before the Arizona border.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Centennial Park (Duncan Town Park cyclist camping)

dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Honest gap: Bylas has no legal established camping. The San Carlos Apache recreation permit (~$7–10/day; buy online at sancarlos.nagfa.net or via vendors; Recreation & Wildlife Dept (928) 475-2343) covers camping only at designated tribal recreation areas — none of which are on US 70 near Bylas — so roadside camping here is NOT legal even with a permit. Realistic plays: (1) call the Recreation & Wildlife Dept in advance and ask specifically about an overnight option for a through-cyclist; (2) arrive early and ask at a church or the police station — riders are regularly hosted; (3) restructure: ride Safford→Globe (~86 mi, gentle US 70 grades) in one day as most ST riders do, or split at Apache Gold Casino RV Park/hotel (~mi 2237, 5 mi east of Globe, tribal-owned, RV $45 and tent policy inconsistent — call (928) 475-7800 range numbers or book the hotel). || UPDATE 2026-08-27: the permit is $10/day (confirmed on scat-nsn.gov) and covers recreation generally, so it is cheap legitimacy for stopping or resting off the shoulder anywhere in those ~60 reservation miles, not just camping. Fourth option worth modelling: end Day 39 at FORT THOMAS (mi 2180) instead of Bylas and ride 69 mi to Globe - verify the reservation boundary first, Fort Thomas sits close to its edge.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Gila County RV Park & Batting Range (downtown Globe)
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: All real options are in/around Globe (mi ~2240–2243), 6–9 mi before the mapped Miami endpoint — Miami itself has no legal camping, only a couple of motels. Plan to stop in Globe; the extra 6 mi to Miami is trivial to make up next morning. Oak Flat CG (free, Tonto NF) is on US 60 toward Superior — the route turns NORTH on AZ 188 before it, so it is NOT relevant unless you're detouring.

All lake campgrounds sit 10–25 mi BEFORE the mapped 2307.5 endpoint — end the day at the lake (Cholla mi ~2295 or Bermuda Flat mi ~2297) rather than the abstract 'near Tonto Basin' point. Budget pick: Bermuda Flat at $8 if you carry water from Globe or the Roosevelt Lake Marina store. Schoolhouse Point was 'Temporarily Closed' as of Aug 2026. Verify Cholla's Oct 1 reopening by phone; Windy Hill (water, $25, confirmed open) is the fail-safe.

Metro Phoenix camping is genuinely awkward: Usery is the only sensible legal tent option and now runs $50 all-in ($40 + $10 reservation fee) after the Jan 2026 county fee hike — over the $35 cap but still the best move. Fiesta RV Resort at the Gilbert endpoint is a 55+ RV resort with no tents — excluded, as are the other age-restricted Mesa resorts. McDowell Mountain Regional Park is 25+ mi off-route (same $40 county rate) — not worth it. If $50 stings, budget motels on US 60/Main St in Mesa run ~$60–85 and Warmshowers hosts are plentiful in Mesa/Gilbert — for a shower, laundry, and real bed before the final push, a motel arguably beats the campground on value here.

dayAdvice.bestBet: White Tank Mountain Regional Park (Willow/semi-developed sites)
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Sun City West itself has zero tent camping — the 55+ RV resorts (e.g., in Sun City/Surprise) don't take tents. Nearest legal camping is White Tank Mountain Regional Park, an ~11-12 mi detour SW. If you don't want to add ~22-24 mi round trip to tomorrow's 73-mi day, take a budget motel in Surprise on the route (Motel 6 / Days Inn cluster on Grand Ave/US-60, typically $60-85 in Nov) and bank the sleep.

Aguila is the thinnest night of this segment: Burro Jim Motel is closed, Constellation Park (Wickenburg) bans tents, and there's no named BLM dispersed area at Aguila (US-60 corridor here is private ag + state trust land, which needs an AZ permit). Plan A: confirm tents at Gladden before leaving Wickenburg. Plan B: stop at Horspitality RV Park near Wickenburg (mi ~2464) and eat the 28-mi shift into tomorrow (Quartzsite day becomes ~88 mi — flat). Plan C: ask at the Aguila community church/school ballfield — small-town courtesy camping is common ST practice, but get explicit permission. Water: buy at Aguila's Family Dollar.

Brawley proper has no tent camping — Palm Lane RV Park is RVs-only. Wiest Lake means ~6 extra miles north (and 6 back south in the morning). If you won't ride the detour after a 68-mi dunes day, take a budget motel on Brawley's Main St/CA-86 (typically $70-95). Skip Glamis camping — the new $55+ weekly vehicle permits and Friday-night OHV chaos make it the worst deal on this segment.

dayAdvice.bestBet: Desert Trails RV Park & Golf Course
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Calexico itself has zero legal camping. Nearby 'options' all fail for tents: Sunbeam Lake RV Resort is RVs-only (300 sites, no tents), Rio Bend RV & Golf Resort is resort-priced with no published tent sites, and Country Life RV Park (mi 2683.2) could not be verified as tent-friendly. Real choices: (1) camp Desert Trails in El Centro at mi ~2684 and finish the last 10 mi next morning, or (2) budget motel in Calexico — several independents plus chains along Imperial Ave (SR-111), typically $65-95 in Nov; El Centro's Motel 6/chain cluster off I-8 runs similar. Book the border-town motel ahead on a Saturday night (Nov 7).

No camping in Jacumba town itself — the renovated Jacumba Hot Springs Hotel (44500 Old Hwy 80) is rooms-only, no tent sites, but sells hot-springs pool passes; a soak there then 2–3 mi to DeAnza is the play. If DeAnza's rate or vibe is off, ride 9 more mi to the Boulevard KOA and bank miles for Day 50.

Alpine itself has NO campground (confirmed — nothing legal in town), and Vacationer RV Resort in El Cajon is verified RVs-only ('Sorry, no tent camping' per their FAQ), so scratch it. Nothing under $40 exists on this stretch: Lake Jennings ($45, right on the onward path, hot showers) is worth the $5 over Green Valley, which sits 15 mi short plus a 3.2-mi climb and freezing 4,000-ft nights. A Warmshowers host in Alpine/El Cajon is the only free play here. || BEST VALUE ON THE CALIFORNIA LEG: Boulder Oaks Campground (Cleveland NF) at mi 2770 — $5 WALK-IN sites with POTABLE WATER, dead on Old Hwy 80 at Buckman Springs Rd, ~27 mi before this endpoint so it falls outside the list below. Compare with $40 at Green Valley, which also costs a 3.2-mi climb off route. Verify the seasonal arroyo-toad closure is lifted.

dayAdvice.bestBet: San Elijo State Beach — Hike & Bike site
Doheny State Beach — Hike & Bike site
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Newport Beach itself has ZERO legal camping — the nearest camp to the Day 52 endpoint is Crystal Cove, 10 mi south. Cleanest budget move: sleep at Doheny hike/bike ($15) at mile ~2898 and accept a 74-mi final day, or pay ~$45 at Crystal Cove Moro to keep the plan's mileage. Huntington by the Sea RV Resort (mi 2924.2) is an RV resort — tent policy unverified and it skews expensive; don't count on it. Newport Dunes Resort allows tents but runs $75+/night.

dayAdvice.bestBet: HI Los Angeles — Santa Monica Hostel
dayAdvice.gapAdvice: Final day — no camp needed at the pier. Dockweiler is verified tent-hostile (RV-only by county rule), so if Grimey wants a roof after the finish it's the HI Santa Monica hostel (~$37–60 dorm, 2 blocks from the pier, 310-393-9913) or nothing budget-friendly; book it before rolling out of Doheny/Crystal Cove.

FL.stateParks: Campsites $16-42/night + tax; primitive camping $5/person where offered. Florida is the ONE state on the route with a formal NO-TURN-AWAY POLICY for self-contained cyclists - a full campground must still take you. Adventure Cycling keeps the policy list; carry a screenshot. Big Lagoon SP (mi 47) is the only park on your Florida miles.
FL.cityParks: Do not count on any. A 2024 state law (HB 1365, effective Oct 1 2024) REQUIRES counties and municipalities to prohibit sleeping or camping on public property. This makes Florida the most legally exposed state on the route for urban or park stealth camping.
FL.dispersed: No national forest on your 13 Florida miles. Blackwater River State Forest is well north of the route.
FL.restAreas: 3-hour parking limit and camping explicitly prohibited (FAC 14-28.002). Not an option.
FL.stealth: Trespass on unposted land generally requires actual notice to leave (FS 810.09), but posted or fenced land is a first-degree misdemeanor - and HB 1365 closes the public-property option. Ride through to Alabama or use Big Lagoon.
FL.notes: Only ~13 route miles, but they are the strictest miles on the trip. Start the day early and get into Alabama.

AL.stateParks: Alabama's segment is short (Perdido Key/Orange Beach to the MS line) but Gulf State Park (Gulf Shores) and Meaher State Park (Spanish Fort, on Mobile Bay) sit essentially on route. Primitive/tent sites vary by park and season — roughly $15-30/night — and every reservation adds a $5.25 (some parks $5.00) non-refundable reservation fee plus a ~4-4.25% nightly 'resort fee'. Reservations run through ReserveAlabama (reserve.alapark.com, 1-800-ALAPARK); walk-ups are accepted when sites are open. Camping includes entry; some parks charge day-users a small gate fee.
AL.cityParks: No city-park camping tradition here — coastal AL municipal parks generally close at dusk by local ordinance and overnight camping is banned unless posted otherwise. With only 1-2 nights in the state and Gulf SP/Meaher SP on route, cyclists rarely need to ask. If stuck near Mobile, call the police non-emergency line rather than stealth-camping in a beach town.
AL.restAreas: Alabama prohibits overnight parking AND camping at its rest areas/welcome centers — the strictest of the Gulf states. The I-10 welcome centers are irrelevant to the bike route anyway. Do not plan any AL rest-area overnight.
AL.publicLands: Effectively zero federal dispersed-camping land on the corridor — no BLM, and Conecuh NF is far north of the route. The Gulf beaches are state/city controlled with camping bans. Treat AL as a paid-campground/Warmshowers state.
AL.notes: Gulf State Park is a resort-priced park (improved sites can run $40-60); its primitive loop is the budget play. Book the Gulf Shores area ahead — snowbird season is ramping up by late September. The AL crossing is 2 days max, so one reservation covers it.

MS.stateParks: The route hugs the coast ~80 mi (Pascagoula-Ocean Springs-Bay St. Louis-Pearlington); Shepard State Park (Gautier) and Buccaneer State Park (Waveland) are both essentially on route. Buccaneer reservable tent sites run ~$28/night; its first-come primitive area is ~$18-20/night. MS state parks reserve through ReserveAmerica (mississippistateparks.reserveamerica.com); walk-up is fine for primitive loops on weekdays. Small per-vehicle day-use fees exist but camping covers entry.
MS.cityParks: Overnight camping in municipal parks is banned by default on the developed Gulf Coast — these are casino/beach towns, not the small-town-hospitality belt. The ask-city-hall tradition doesn't really operate here. With two well-placed state parks, the coast is easy to cover legally.
MS.restAreas: MDOT allows overnight PARKING but no camping — vehicles parked over ~8 continuous hours are considered long-term and can be removed by MDOT or Highway Patrol, and 'recreational camping' (tents, gear out) is explicitly disallowed. Not usable for a cyclist with a tent.
MS.publicLands: De Soto National Forest (free dispersed camping, 14-day limit) lies ~20-30 miles north of the coastal route — the corridor does not touch it, and detouring costs a day. Coastal land is state/private. Skip it unless rerouting inland.
MS.notes: Buccaneer SP in Waveland is the classic pre-New Orleans overnight (day's ride to the city). Fall is shoulder season on the coast — sites are gettable, but check tropical-weather closures; these low-lying parks shut for storms. MDWFP phone numbers answer fee questions faster than the website.

LA.stateParks: Unimproved (no-hookup) sites run $18-27/night + tax, improved $28-42; a $4.50 non-refundable reservation fee applies to every booking including walk-ins, and there's a $3/person day-use fee for non-campers. Reservations via lastateparks.com / 1-833-609-0686, and the system explicitly welcomes walk-ups when sites are open. On or near route: Fontainebleau and Fairview-Riverside (Mandeville, north shore) and Bayou Segnette (Westwego, across from New Orleans); Lake Fausse Pointe sits near the New Iberia stretch.
LA.cityParks: This is where the ask-the-town tradition begins: Cajun-country towns (Donaldsonville-Morgan City-Eunice-Kinder-DeRidder-Merryville belt) have a history of letting touring cyclists pitch in town parks or under pavilions with permission. Default law is still no-overnight-camping in municipal parks unless posted or permitted — so call city hall before 4:30pm or the police non-emergency line, get a name, set up late, leave early. ACA map panels mark several cyclist-tolerant town parks in this stretch.
LA.restAreas: Louisiana has no statewide overnight statute, but the practical rule is no overnight parking or camping at rest areas — several I-10 facilities post limits or close overnight, and tents are out everywhere. Don't build LA rest areas into the plan.
LA.publicLands: Kisatchie NF is far north of the corridor — not reachable. The real LA public-land option is Wildlife Management Areas: camping is free of nightly fees but ONLY in designated areas, max 16 consecutive days per 30 (then 48 hours out), and you need a WMA Access Permit (included with LA hunting/fishing licenses, free under 18) plus a WMA Camping Permit per party at LDWF campgrounds; a Self-Clearing Permit covers most other WMA activities. Check which WMAs sit near the route (e.g., Atchafalaya-basin areas) before counting on one.
LA.notes: Buying the cheapest LDWF license/stamp that carries WMA access is the legal key to free WMA camping — sort it online before arriving. October-January is gun season on WMAs: designated camp areas fill with hunters and blaze orange is essential. New Orleans itself = Warmshowers or hostel territory; there is no legal cheap camping in the city.

TX.stateParks: Texas is the only state on the route that stacks a per-person daily ENTRANCE fee ($3-8/person/day, e.g. $4 at Seminole Canyon) on top of the site fee — and it's charged for every day you're in the park. Tent/primitive sites run $10-15 (Seminole Canyon: primitive $10, water sites $15), electric $20-25. Reservations through the Texas State Parks Reservation System (tpwd.texas.gov, 512-389-8900), 5-month rolling window; walk-ups get unreserved sites. The $70 State Parks Pass kills all entrance fees — only worth it if you'll log ~10+ park-days crossing the state.
TX.cityParks: Texas is the heart of the Southern Tier city-park tradition: many small West/South Texas towns officially or informally let cyclists camp in the city park — some post it, some run $5-10 honor boxes, most just expect you to check in at city hall (before close) or the police/sheriff non-emergency line. Legally, overnight camping in a municipal park is prohibited unless the town allows it, so the phone call IS the legal cover; get the officer's or clerk's name. This works far better in 1,000-person towns than in cities.
TX.restAreas: TxDOT allows a 24-hour stay at rest areas, picnic areas, and travel information centers — but Transp. Code 545.411 makes erecting a tent, shelter, or structure an offense, and sleeping must happen inside a vehicle. Cyclists do quietly overnight at remote West Texas picnic areas (there's no vehicle to sleep in), but know it's technically illegal — cowboy-camp without the tent, arrive at dusk, leave at dawn, and have a fallback.
TX.publicLands: Texas is ~95% private land — essentially no BLM or National Forest anywhere near the corridor, and fences run to the highway shoulder. The one federal bright spot is Amistad National Recreation Area at Del Rio (NPS): cheap primitive first-come campgrounds right off the route. Otherwise the TX toolkit is state parks (Seminole Canyon, Davis Mountains-area), city parks, and RV parks that take tents.
TX.notes: Budget for the entrance-fee stacking — a $10 primitive site is really $14-18/night solo. West of Del Rio the gaps get serious (Comstock-Sanderson-Marathon); the sheriff check-in habit doubles as a safety net out there. Never camp on roadside land that isn't a signed public facility — trespassing on Texas ranchland is taken seriously.

NM.stateParks: Since Jan 1, 2025: primitive camping $10/night residents / $15 non-residents, developed sites $15/$20, hookups extra ($10 electric, $5 water/sewer) — fees are per vehicle per day and explicitly include walk-in and BICYCLE campers. Reservations via ReserveAmerica (newmexicostateparks.reserveamerica.com, 1-877-664-7787), $3.50/night reservation fee capped at $10; first-come sites remain at most parks. On route: Leasburg Dam (near Las Cruces), then Percha Dam and Caballo Lake SPs right on the approach to Hillsboro/Emory Pass, and City of Rocks SP between Silver City and Deming.
NM.cityParks: Less of an institution than Texas, but the same ask-first protocol works in villages like Hatch and Hillsboro — default ordinance position is no overnight in town parks without permission. Small-town NM is generally cyclist-tolerant on this corridor since the ACA route is known. Police non-emergency or village office before 5pm.
NM.restAreas: NMDOT rest areas allow up to 24 hours and overnight parking, but no camping and no sleeping outside a vehicle — so no tents. Same practical situation as Texas: not a legal tent option for a cyclist.
NM.publicLands: The best public-land stretch on the whole route: BLM land around Las Cruces (Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks NM area) allows free dispersed camping, and the Gila National Forest over Emory Pass (NM-152, Black Range) allows free dispersed camping forest-wide — 14-day limit per 30 days, camp 100 ft from water, existing fire rings, no permit needed. Iron Creek Campground and other NFS sites sit right on the Emory Pass climb.
NM.notes: Non-resident pricing means a solo cyclist pays $15 even for primitive state-park sites — Gila NF dispersed camping is free and directly on route, so use it over Emory Pass. Nights above 7,000 ft in late October are below freezing; Emory Pass tops at 8,228 ft. Fall gun deer seasons run in the Gila — orange on the tent.

AZ.stateParks: AZ State Parks camping runs $25-50/night (tent/non-hookup sites typically at the low end), plus a $3.60 non-refundable reservation fee; book at azstateparks.com up to 13 months out, walk-ups OK when open. Fees rose Feb 25, 2025, and the all-parks annual pass jumped to $200 — irrelevant for a pass-through cyclist. On route: Roper Lake SP (Safford) and Lost Dutchman SP (Apache Junction); note some AZ parks also charge per-vehicle day-use that camping covers.
AZ.cityParks: Arizona towns generally ban camping in municipal parks and, post-Grants Pass (2024), metro-Phoenix-area ordinances are actively enforced — do not try it in the Valley. Small towns on the eastern segment (Duncan, Pima) have been known to host cyclists at town parks with a call ahead — Duncan in particular has cyclist lore — but always ask city hall/marshal first. Outside towns, public land is so abundant that city parks matter less here.
AZ.restAreas: ADOT rest areas permit overnight parking with no posted maximum, but camping (tents, gear outside a vehicle) is prohibited. Same story: fine for motorists, not a tent option.
AZ.publicLands: Excellent: Coronado NF near Safford, then Tonto NF from Globe through Superior toward Apache Junction (free dispersed camping, 14-day/30 limit; free first-come Oak Flat CG area near Superior sits close to US 60), and wide-open BLM in the west (Harquahala/Ranegras plains around Salome-Hope-Brenda; La Posa LTVA at Quartzsite is near the I-10 corridor). Standard BLM dispersed rules: free, 14 days per 28 within 25 miles, use existing sites. Also note AZ State Trust Land checkerboards much of the desert — that requires its own permit.
AZ.notes: Arizona State Trust land (unfenced desert that looks like BLM) legally requires a $15/year individual recreation permit (14 camping nights/yr, buy online at land.az.gov) — either buy one or verify you're on true BLM before pitching. Metro Phoenix is a 2-day no-camping gauntlet: plan Warmshowers/motel for Apache Junction-Tempe-Wickenburg. Check Tonto NF fire restrictions — fall can still be stage 1/2.

CA.stateParks: The budget crown jewel: coastal CA state parks offer first-come, first-served hike/bike sites at a per-person fee — currently $10-15/person/night (San Elijo SB charges $15), no reservation possible or needed, 1-2 night max (San Elijo: 2 nights, 10 days/yr). On the San Diego→LA leg that means San Elijo SB, South Carlsbad SB, San Onofre/San Mateo, Doheny SB, and Crystal Cove — arrive by mid-afternoon. Standard reservable sites (ReserveCalifornia) run $35-60+ on this coast, so hike/bike is the play. The desert segment (Blythe→Jacumba) has no state parks on route.
CA.cityParks: Do not attempt city-park camping in Southern California — municipal anti-camping ordinances are aggressively enforced in San Diego, Orange County, and LA, and the small-town-hospitality tradition does not exist here. The hike/bike network exists precisely so cyclists don't need it. In the Imperial Valley towns (Brawley, El Centro), use motels or nearby BLM instead.
CA.restAreas: Caltrans: 8-hour maximum stay per rest area per 24 hours, no camping, no tents, must be inside a vehicle — sleeping on a bench or the ground counts as camping (21 CCR 2205). Also explicitly no parking at rest areas while off biking. Zero utility for a touring cyclist.
CA.publicLands: The desert third is nearly all BLM: free 14-day dispersed camping around Palo Verde, the Imperial Sand Dunes area (Glamis), and the Yuha Desert; plus seven Long-Term Visitor Areas including Hot Spring LTVA near Holtville (right off the route, with an actual hot tub-spring). Then the Cleveland NF (Pine Valley/Descanso district): dispersed 'remote camping' requires a free permit emailed to the district ~2 days ahead, wood/charcoal fires are banned outside developed sites, and Boulder Oaks CG (recreation.gov) sits on old US-80 on route.
CA.notes: LTVA season runs Sept 15-Apr 15: inside LTVA boundaries you need a permit ($40/any 14 days, $180 season), but ordinary BLM outside LTVAs stays free — for one-night stops, camp outside the LTVA line or pay the $40 if you want the Holtville hot spring + trash service. Get the Descanso district remote-camping permit before leaving El Centro if you want to disperse in the Laguna/Pine Valley mountains. After San Diego, budget = hike/bike sites the whole way to LA.

programs.warmshowers: Warmshowers.org is the reciprocal hospitality network of touring cyclists hosting touring cyclists (bed or yard, shower, often dinner) — free to stay, with a one-time ~$30 signup contribution for new members; the website is free to use after that, while the mobile app charges cyclists a separate subscription (~$2.99/mo or $17.99/yr) unless used in host-only mode. Send personalized requests ~3-7 days ahead with a check-in message the day before; same-day requests work sometimes but are poor etiquette. Density on the Southern Tier is good in and around cities (New Orleans, Lafayette, Austin-adjacent, El Paso, Las Cruces, Silver City, Tucson/Phoenix, San Diego) and thin-to-absent across west Texas and the desert gaps — plan hosts for the expensive metros, camping for the empty stretches.
programs.churches: The ACA Southern Tier maps mark churches that have historically welcomed cyclists (lawn camping, sometimes a hall floor and shower), concentrated in the Bible-belt half — Louisiana through west Texas — and mostly Baptist and Methodist congregations in small towns. The norm: call the church office mid-afternoon (or knock), ask for the pastor or secretary, say you're a touring cyclist on the Adventure Cycling route and ask if you may pitch a tent on their grounds for one night; offer a donation and leave the site spotless. Unannounced Sunday-evening arrivals are the one timing that reliably works without a call, since people are on site.
programs.fireStations: The small-town check-in is a real institution on rural US bike routes: stop at the fire station, city hall, or sheriff's office in the late afternoon, explain you're a cross-country cyclist, and ask where they'd like you to camp — the answer is usually the city park, the fairgrounds, behind the station, or a churchyard, and the check-in itself is your legal cover plus insurance against a 2am flashlight wake-up. Volunteer fire stations in Texas and Louisiana sometimes offer water, a hose shower, or a bay floor. Always get the name of whoever said yes, arrive/settle before dark, and be gone by 7-8am.
programs.adventureCycling: Adventure Cycling's Southern Tier map set (paper + Bicycle Route Navigator app) lists campgrounds, city parks that allow camping, cyclist-friendly churches, hostels, and full service directories per map panel; the free online Route Updates & Corrections (addenda) pages carry current closures, rerouting, and camping changes reported by riders, and the Route Feedback Form feeds them. ACA's forums and the route resources pages also carry section-by-section riding-conditions notes (terrain, service gaps, water warnings). Cross-check any pre-2024 addenda against the current map edition since the route was revised.
programs.apps: For this corridor: iOverlander (free, community-sourced) is the strongest in the desert West — wild spots, water spigots, and 'asked-permission' town spots with recent check-ins; freecampsites.net (free website) is best for finding legal free options like TX picnic areas, city parks, and BLM pull-offs east of the Rockies; The Dyrt's free tier is the biggest campground database and fine for looking up state-park loops; Campendium is useful for BLM/LTVA and rest-area reviews though more features have moved behind Roadpass paywalls. Practical combo: iOverlander + freecampsites.net, both cached offline before the west-Texas and desert segments.
programs.campPendleton: SUSPENDED as of Aug 2026: 'New issuances and renewals are temporarily suspended... until the Trusted Traveler program is reinstated.' Existing passes stay valid to their printed expiration. Falls on Day 52. Plan the outside-the-fence route - coastal bike path from San Onofre to Las Pulgas, then the bicycle-permitted I-5 shoulder to Oceanside Harbor Dr. Re-check before you get there: Visitor Center 760-763-8435. https://www.pendleton.marines.mil/Staff/Principal-Staff/Security-and-Emergency-Services/Base-Access/
programs.acaSection1Detour: Adventure Cycling publishes an official Southern Tier Section 1 detour that avoids SR-78 between Brawley and Blythe over truck-traffic and shoulder hazards - the corridor your Days 46-47 ride. The detour swaps in an I-8/Yuma line whose camping is BLM Long Term Visitor Areas (Holtville Hot Springs, LTVAs between Holtville and Yuma), Mittry Lake Wildlife Area, and Dateland RV Park. Your route follows the classic line - make that a decision, not an accident. https://www.adventurecycling.org/routes-and-maps/route-alerts/major-detour-on-southern-tier-section-1/

generalTips: Sunset math: by late October you'll lose light by 5:15-5:45pm (Mountain/Pacific) — plan to be AT camp by 4:30, which also matches the city-hall/sheriff check-in window (offices close 4:30-5:00).

Texas fee stacking is the hidden cost: a $10 primitive site + $4-8/person entrance fee makes state parks $14-18/night solo — count your planned TX park nights before buying the $70 annual pass (breakeven ~10-14 park-days for one person).

Buy the cheap legal permits before you need them: an LDWF license/permit with WMA access (free designated-area camping in Louisiana) and the $15/yr Arizona State Trust Land recreation permit — both purchasable online, both turn 'trespassing' into 'legal free camping'.

Free camping center of gravity: from Las Cruces westward, default to BLM and National Forest dispersed camping (free, 14-day limits, no permit except Cleveland NF's Descanso district, which needs a free emailed permit ~2 days ahead) and save paid sites for towns.

You arrive in LTVA country (Quartzsite/Blythe/Holtville) after the Sept 15 season opens: camp on regular BLM just OUTSIDE the LTVA boundaries for free, or pay $40 for any-14-days if you want the Hot Spring LTVA's spring, trash, and company.

October-November is gun deer season in every state you cross — on WMAs and National Forests wear blaze orange while riding and drape something orange on the tent, and avoid camping near feeders, food plots, or at dawn shooting light.

Rest areas are a vehicle-sleeper's game, not a tent camper's: every state on this route bans tents at rest areas (CA even caps stays at 8 hours), so treat TX/NM picnic-area overnights as no-tent, dusk-to-dawn, fallback-only moves.

Water is the desert budget item that isn't money: 100+ mile gaps in west Texas (Comstock-Sanderson-Marathon) and the AZ/CA desert demand 6-10L capacity; use iOverlander water POIs, and cemeteries, churches, and fire stations reliably have spigots.
Spend your Warmshowers requests on the expensive metros — New Orleans, El Paso, Phoenix, San Diego — where legal camping is nonexistent and motels are $100+; camp the cheap rural stretches instead.

After San Diego, the coastal hike/bike system ($10-15/person, first-come, no reservations possible) is your entire San Diego→LA lodging plan: San Elijo, South Carlsbad, San Onofre, Doheny, Crystal Cove — roll in by 2-3pm, respect the 1-2 night max.

Louisiana runs on civic hospitality, not campgrounds: a fire station (Bunkie, mi 552), a tourism office with showers (Oberlin, mi 616), a church (Simmesport, mi 522) and two museum/visitor-center sites in Merryville (mi 671-675) are all free and all confirmed active in 2025. That is five free nights in one state if you ask.

The church ask has a technique: call the number on the church SIGN on a weekday MORNING (rural offices are staffed roughly Mon-Thu 9-2), and ask for the LAWN, not the building - the invitation inside usually follows. Riders report it works about half the time, which is plenty when you stack it with parks and picnic areas.
Two nights on this plan are worth booking rather than winging: Day 53 into Santa Monica (no legal camping on the last 52 mi) and any Marfa night now that El Cosmico has closed.

guide.title: Sleeping cheap on this route
guide.intro: Nobody camps free coast to coast on one trick. Riders who spend almost nothing stack six moves, and each move owns a different stretch of this route. This is the strategy layer; the Nights tab is the per-day answer.

items.body: The east half runs on institutions that host cyclists on purpose: a fire station's couches (Bunkie, mi 552), a tourism office's field with showers (Oberlin, mi 616), a church fellowship hall (Simmesport, mi 522), a museum cyclist bunk room and a visitors center (Merryville, mi 671-675), community-center grounds (Langtry, mi 1418). Free, legal, and confirmed active in 2025. That is five free nights in Louisiana alone if you ask.

Baptist and Methodist churches across Louisiana and Texas host riders indoors. Sanderson's First Baptist fed a 2025 group and lent the pastor's shower. Call the number on the church sign on a weekday morning, and ask for the lawn rather than the building — the invitation inside usually follows. See the church playbook below.

Texas Transportation Code 545.411 gives you up to 24 hours at any TxDOT rest area, picnic area, roadside park or scenic overlook. Erecting a tent is barred on paper, but an offense requires a posted sign or an officer's notice plus 8 hours to comply — so riders cowboy-camp, or pitch at dusk and strike at dawn. This is how everyone crosses Del Rio to El Paso. None of these have water.

From Emory Pass west the game flips: BLM and national-forest land is free for 14 days at a stretch, no permit. Free developed campgrounds sit directly on your line — Iron Creek (mi 1986), Railroad Canyon (1988), Upper Gallinas (1991), Tonto NF around Tonto Basin (~2308), and the Quartzsite BLM areas Hi Jolly (2550) and Dome Rock (2557). The west is the cheap half of this trip, not the expensive one.

California state beaches hold first-come hike/bike sites you cannot be turned away from for lack of a reservation. $15 per person, register after 2 PM, out by noon, two nights max per park. San Elijo (mi 2855) through Crystal Cove (2911) — your Day 52 passes every one of them. After Crystal Cove there is nothing legal for 60 miles.

Roughly $30 one-time for lifetime access, 200,000+ members. Hosts cluster exactly where camping is illegal: New Orleans, Austin, El Paso, Las Cruces, Silver City, Phoenix, San Diego, LA. Message one to two days ahead and send several requests at once. It is the cheapest lodging insurance you can buy for this route.

sections.title: What this actually costs
sections.intro: A realistic mix based on what 2023-2026 riders did, with weather bail-outs budgeted in rather than wished away.

ledger.what: Free — civic stops, churches, picnic areas, BLM and forest dirt, town parks
Cheap camps — Merryville, Shepherd, Fort Clark, Marathon, state parks, hiker/biker
Motel bail-outs — storms, heat, the no-option towns

sections.total: about $765 for 52 nights, plus the one-time $30 Warmshowers join

items.body: A motel every night runs $6,000-10,000. Even doubling the bail-out nights on this plan lands near $1,250. The Nights tab's own estimate, taking the cheapest option every night, comes in lower still — but that assumes perfect weather and no rest days, which is not a trip.

sections.title: Where your route leaves the ACA line
sections.intro: Your route is a reconstruction and in four places it departs the classic Southern Tier. Guidebooks and journals will recommend stops that are not on your road. Verified by measuring each spot against your own route geometry.

items.body: The classic line runs Bogalusa to Franklinton to Jackson. Yours dips south through New Orleans and Donaldsonville, crosses at the Audubon Bridge and heads up through Angola. Franklinton's police-department host is 17 miles off your line; Bogalusa (mi 250) is the on-route town.

items.h: New Mexico to Arizona — via Lordsburg, not AZ-78
items.body: The classic road goes Silver City to Cliff to Mule Creek down AZ-78 into Duncan, which is why every guide raves about the free Black Jack and Coal Creek campgrounds and Bill Evans Lake. Yours goes Silver City to Lordsburg to Duncan on US-70. Those three free camps are 13 to 23 miles off your road. Lordsburg's free Veterans Park (mi 2074) is your substitute.

items.h: Arizona — via Tonto Basin, not Superior
items.body: The classic route runs Globe to Superior to Apache Junction. Yours turns north through Tonto Basin into Gilbert. That trades away Oak Flat (15-18 mi off, and private land since March 2026) and Lost Dutchman, and trades in genuine Tonto NF dispersed camping around Tonto Basin.

You run Brawley to Calexico to Jacumba. Ocotillo is still on your line at mi 2728. Glamis is squarely on route at mi 2637, so the Imperial Sand Dunes permit question is unavoidable rather than optional — and Halloween and Thanksgiving weekends bring tens of thousands of OHVs through there.

sections.title: How to actually get a church stay
sections.intro: This is not begging and it is not a gamble. On this route it is an established custom riders have used for decades. It has a technique.

items.body: Call the number on the church sign on a weekday morning. Rural offices keep tiny hours — typically Monday to Thursday, 9 to 2 — so an afternoon call reaches nobody. Riders who do this report it works about half the time, which is plenty when you are stacking it with parks and picnic areas.

Ask for the lawn, not the building. A working script from a couple who was never refused: "Hi! We're biking across the country and we're scheduled to come through town this evening. We were wondering if we could set up our tent on your land." It is a modest ask and an easy yes, and the invitation to come inside follows more often than not.

On this route the yeses cluster Baptist and Methodist, plus non-denominational community churches. Wednesday evenings mean church activities, so arriving then can land you in a potluck. Saturday night into Sunday is the one to avoid unless they explicitly bless it — the hall is needed Sunday morning.

Leave a donation in the plate, leave the room cleaner than you found it, and accept the invitation to the service if it comes. Bunkie's fire station has exactly one house rule — cyclists must shower — which tells you what hosts actually care about.

The same ask works on the rest of small-town civic life, and on this route those have receipts: police departments, fire stations, tourism offices, museums, community centers, and city hall for the town park. Ask the sheriff's non-emergency line where a cyclist can pitch a tent tonight and you will usually get an answer rather than a lecture.

Experienced riders warn against making churches the primary plan. Make them one layer of six. The nights this data cannot anchor are exactly the nights you will be glad you also had a picnic area, a BLM map, and a Warmshowers thread going.

sections.title: Before you roll out of Pensacola

items.body: About $30 one-time, lifetime. Covers precisely the cities where camping is illegal. Buy it before you need it.

items.h: Pull the free California campfire permit
items.body: Free online quiz, required to run a stove on Forest Service, BLM or state land in California. Separately, email the Cleveland NF Descanso district for their free remote-camping permit (about two days) if you want a dispersed night there. Wood and charcoal fires are banned outside developed campgrounds in that forest.

items.h: Buy the $10 San Carlos tribal recreation permit
items.body: sancarlos.nagfa.net. Cheap legitimacy for the 60 reservation miles on Day 39 — it covers stopping, resting off the shoulder and photographing, not just camping.
FreeRoam's land-ownership layer answers the question that matters every night from Las Cruces west: is this dirt BLM, or is it somebody's ranch?
Most documented camps on this route are concrete pads, picnic slabs, church lawns and rock-hard desert. Ground beyond the picnic pads in west Texas is described as rock hard, thorny and rocky.

items.h: Blaze orange if you pass in fall
items.body: Gun deer season runs roughly October to January across the southern states, and the free forest camping overlaps it. Big Thicket restricts backcountry camping to non-hunting areas October 1 to February 28; Conecuh NF needs written district permission during gun season.

items.h: Four calls worth making a week out
items.body: Merryville museum (337) 825-0101 · Oberlin tourism (337) 639-4868 · Sanderson First Baptist via the visitor center (432) 345-2324 · Shepherd Sanctuary (281) 705-2581. These are the stops that make a whole week easier.

sections.title: What the calendar does to this plan

items.h: Your first two weeks sit inside peak hurricane season
items.body: Atlantic season runs through November 30 and the Gulf legs are the exposed part. A 2025 group lost two days storm-bound in Simmesport, sheltering in the church. A 2026 rider got stranded at Fort Morgan when a blowout tide killed the ferry. This is the argument for spare days.

items.h: The desert wants you late, the pass wants you early
items.body: Phoenix, Blythe and Brawley still hit 95-105F into mid-October. But Emory Pass tops out at 8,228 ft and its free campgrounds sit at 6,500-7,300 ft, where nights drop below freezing from late October and NM-152 can see snow in November. The window where both work is roughly late October into mid-November, and crossing Emory Pass before mid-November is the harder constraint.

items.h: Fall is the easy season on the coast
items.body: Post-Labor Day the first-come hiker/biker sites stop being competitive. Quartzsite's free BLM areas are near-empty in October and November; the snowbird crush does not arrive until January. The back half of this ride is timed well.
